segments.narration: One animal killed over sixty people in three years. It hunted a single corner of France and would not stop.
The attacks began in Gevaudan in summer 1764 and ran for three years, across ninety kilometres of mountains. Reports counted over two hundred attacks.
Louis XV sent soldiers, then professional wolf hunters with eight bloodhounds, then his own hunter Francois Antoine. How does one animal beat all of them?
Antoine shot a huge grey wolf in September 1765, sixty kilos and nearly two metres long, and was paid nine thousand livres. The attacks started again.
A local hunter, Jean Chastel, killed the last one in June 1767. Historians now think it was never one monster, just wolves, and a province that had stopped sleeping.

verdicts.claim: Estimates of the Beast of Gevaudan's death toll run from about 60 to 113 people over roughly three years.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia cites a 1987 study counting 113 deaths and notes other sources give 60 to 100. The narration says 'over sixty', which is true on every published estimate rather than picking one disputed figure.

verdicts.claim: The attacks ran from 30 June 1764 to 19 June 1767 over an area of roughly 90 by 80 km in the Margeride Mountains of the former province of Gevaudan, and a 1987 study counted 210 attacks.
verdicts.note: 69% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 8 number(s)

verdicts.claim: Louis XV sent a force under Captain Duhamel, then the professional wolf hunters Jean-Charles d'Enneval and his son with eight bloodhounds, then his hunter Francois Antoine, who reached Le Malzieu on 22 June 1765.
verdicts.note: 91% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 2 number(s)

verdicts.claim: Antoine killed a large grey wolf, the Loup de Chazes, on 20-21 September 1765 - about 1.7 m long and 60 kg - and received over 9,000 livres, but attacks resumed afterwards.
verdicts.note: 94% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 7 number(s)

verdicts.claim: Jean Chastel shot the animal on 19 June 1767 on Mont Mouchet, and most modern scholars attribute the deaths to one or more wolves, with public hysteria spreading belief in a single monster.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia: Chastel shot it on 19 June 1767 on Mont Mouchet; most modern scholars attribute the deaths to one or more wolves or wolf packs, with public hysteria spreading the supernatural account. The narration deliberately omits the silver bullet, which Wikipedia calls a literary invention.
